tier_reason: Peer-reviewed CCS 2017 paper (arXiv 1709.02746) would support B, but arxiv.org, ar5iv, deepai, the West Point repository copy and the co-author's site were all unreachable (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the numbers were seen only in WebSearch snippets of the paper; the repo carries no benchmark code or results. Held at C per the precedent for papers that could not be opened.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Seen only in WebSearch snippets of the CCS 2017 paper: FreeGuard averages 1.8% runtime overhead (arithmetic mean; 1.4% geometric mean) relative to the default Linux (glibc) allocator over 19 multithreaded applications; the paper's introduction gives OpenBSD malloc 22% overhead and DieHarder over 36% slower runtime on average. A later patent for the group's Guarder allocator quotes DieHarder 74%, OpenBSD 31% and FreeGuard 1% from a different setup. The win is against secure allocators (DieHarder, OpenBSD); against glibc it is near parity (about 2% slower), not faster.
corrections.workload: Average runtime overhead relative to the default Linux allocator over 19 multithreaded applications: 11 from PARSEC plus real applications including Apache, Firefox and MySQL (per search snippets of the paper; the full list was not read). OpenBSD malloc run with junking level 0 and DieHarder (08/05/2017 version) with heap multiplier 8/7 and destroy-on-free on, per the snippets.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org, ar5iv, deepai, the West Point copy, the co-author's site, usenix.net and patents.justia.com were unreachable, so the paper's evaluation section was never opened and every number comes from WebSearch result summaries. Hardware (Xeon E5-2640) and compiler (GCC 4.9.1 -O2) come from earlier snippets and were not confirmed in this verification. The repo has no paper, benchmark scripts or results (6 commits, no benchmark directory); the README only cites the CCS 2017 paper and makes unquantified 'dramatically improve performance' claims. A peer-reviewed paper would normally rate tier B; held at C because the numbers could not be read at the source. The claim against glibc is parity (1.8% average overhead), the speed win is only against other secure allocators (DieHarder, OpenBSD); DieHarder still enables destroy-on-free while FreeGuard and OpenBSD do not, so the comparison is not security-equivalent. Figures differ between the paper (OpenBSD 22%, DieHarder >36%) and later Guarder material (31%, 74%), which used a different setup. Authors' own implementation and measurement. No commits since 2018-01-04; the same group's successor is UTSASRG/Guarder.

notes: Repo checked on github.com: GPL-2.0 (README also offers commercial licensing via UTSA), 38 stars, 6 commits, last commit 2018-01-04, not archived, not a fork; maintenance corrected to abandoned (>3 years). Benchmark URL (arXiv) is live but blocked from this session; a verifier with arXiv access could raise this to B after reading the evaluation section.

tier_reason: Author's own project page shows tables of Bstrlib vs C library string.h and CBString vs std::string with compilers and CPUs (Athlon XP 1.62 GHz, Power 4 1 GHz) named, but flags for those runs are not stated; benchmark sources (cbench.c, cppbench.cpp) exist only in a 2006 SourceForge examples archive that postdates the 2004-era runs. First-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Per column: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c with STLport, Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0 (4.0 99026), GNU gcc/g++ 3.3.3 (Cygwin), GNU gcc/g++ 3.3.3 (SUSE Linux). Flags used for the published numbers are not stated; the page only says Bstrlib must be built at a maximum optimisation setting such as -O2. The later SourceForge examples archive (examples-09282006.zip) ships makefiles with gcc -O3 -Wall -pedantic -ansi -s (Makefile.gccXnix), MSVC /O2 /Ob2 (Makefile.msvc), Intel /Ox /Ob2 (Makefile.intel) and WATCOM -oairten -6r (Makefile.watcom), but it is not known that these were used for the page's runs.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the author's project page, run on 2004-era compilers (gcc 3.3.3, VC++ 6.0, Intel C++ 6.0, WATCOM 11.0c) and CPUs (Athlon XP, Power 4), so they say little about current libstdc++, libc++ or glibc. Flags for the published runs are not stated. The page's benchmark links point to the dead SourceForge CVS viewer and the sources are not in the GitHub repo; cbench.c and cppbench.cpp (2006 versions) are in the SourceForge examples archive examples-09282006.zip (bstring/files/examples/ex10), which may differ from the code that produced the 2004-era numbers. The enormous C-API concatenation ratios come from cbench.c's testCSTR_concat, which calls strcat 500 times into one growing buffer (re-scanning the destination each call, quadratic) against Bstrlib's length-tracked bconcat, so they reflect the idiom, not general speed; the CBString vs std::string concatenation test uses the same += idiom on both sides, and its 21100%/19400% gaps on VC++ 6.0/Intel 6.0 reflect that era's Microsoft STL, as the author notes. On gcc (SUSE) the C API is slower than the C library for assignment (91%), scan (89%) and replace (86%), and on gcc Cygwin for assignment (89%); CBString is slower than STLport for character extraction (63% WATCOM) and assignment (93% WATCOM). Default construction is far slower than std::string per the page. Column for g++ SUSE ran on a different CPU (Power 4) than the other four (Athlon XP). Timing uses clock() over about 2 seconds per test, single run. bstrlib.txt also claims bsreadln can be 'several times faster' than fgets, with no numbers. Last commit 2016-11-02; the README calls the library stable and well tested but does not declare it complete. Repo also ships gpl.txt (dual BSD/GPL licensing).

notes: All claimed_speedup percentages match the features.html tables and column/CPU mapping (Athlon XP colspan 4, Power 4 for SUSE). maintenance_status corrected from finished to abandoned (last commit 2016-11-02, README says stable but not complete); BSD-3-Clause, 572 stars, not archived or a fork confirmed on github.com.
